item.title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
item.description:
Image caption,
Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's electionByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondent, Reporting fromNazarethPublished4 hours ago
At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.
Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."
Image caption,
All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab parties
Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.
If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.
A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

item.title: Celebrity shark guided out of South Korea canal refuses to swim out to sea
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canalByJake Kwon, Reporting fromBusan, and Koh EwePublished22 October 2026, 05:12 BSTUpdated 7 minutes ago
A famed dusky shark in South Korea is still lingering near a canal that it was guided out of on Wednesday.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month. For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get it back to the open sea using large nets.
On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and has been circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway.
Its rescue prompted mixed reactions in Busan, where some said the shark should stay while others felt it was better for it to go.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark.
But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities.
For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal.
Rescuers freed it by removing the outer layer, and have since fortified the remaining layer of nets to prevent it from going back in.
Since then, authorities said, Bukangi has been swimming further out but keeps circling back.
A government official told the BBC on Thursday afternoon that rescuers had concluded their operations to free the shark.

item.title: Two killed in attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Dammam is the largest city in Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern ProvinceByDavid GrittenPublished1 hour ago
Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says.
Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals.
The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles.
On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze.
It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.
Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.

item.title: Police investigate Married at First Sight Australia after 'inappropriate' allegations
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentPublished35 minutes ago
Married at First Sight Australia is facing fresh controversy after police launched an investigation into the hit reality TV show.
New South Wales told BBC News that inquiries had taken place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".
Channel Nine, which broadcasts Married at First Sight Australia, confirmed that it was "aware of a police investigation" involving the show's production company.
It is the latest blow for the show, after a BBC News investigation earlier this year into MAFS Australia revealed cast members said they had not been told their partners had previous drug and violence convictions.
Those revelations led to a warning from Australia's media watchdog, which called them "serious and disturbing".
The British version of Married at First Sight, known to many as MAFS UK, was separately plunged into crisis in May after BBC Panorama reported rape allegations from two female cast members - allegations the men involved have denied.
MAFS UK is made by a different production company to the Australian version.
The Dark Side of Married at First Sight
Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.

Married at First Sight shows single people agreeing to "marry" total strangers after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.
The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on "honeymoons", before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day.

item.title: El Salvador's president threatens Haitian gangs over military hostages
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByJamie Whitehead Published5 minutes ago
El Salvador's president has said he has launched a military operation to rescue four air force personnel who have been missing in Haiti since Sunday.
Nayib Bukele wrote in a post on X that Wednesday's attack was "nothing" compared with what would happen if all the hostages - who he said were not combatants - were not returned alive.
They went missing after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups," El Salvador's armed forces said. The ambush occurred in Croix-des-Bouquets, an area controlled by armed groups.
They were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), approved by the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, to tackle escalating gang violence in Haiti.
According to Bukele, the mission consisted of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary jobs were to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
His post said the Salvadoran military operation's single objective was to bring the four men back home alive.
He added that if all four were returned alive, without being harmed, "everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping".
Bukele added they were kidnapped "in a cowardly manner" while returning after buying food at a market in the area.
A statement released by the Armed Forces of El Salvador on Sunday said the group was ambushed while travelling back to its camp in an armoured vehicle, which caught fire after being hit by explosives.
So far, no gang has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Salvadoran helicopters were deployed to assist, with multiple attempts to make an approach by land and air hampered by fighting and local security conditions, the armed forces said.
On Wednesday, before Bukele announced the launch of the military operation, the GSF said it was searching for the four missing personnel following the attack.

item.title: Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
item.description:
Image source, Christoph GreztmacherImage caption,
Eva Greztmacher, 76, had spent many years in Niger as an aid workerByBasillioh RukangaPublished2 hours ago
Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.
Austrian national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Swiss Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.
No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.
Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.
Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.
Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.
Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.
A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.
Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.

item.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian citiesByJaroslav LukivPublished21 October 2026
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.
The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.
Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."
The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.
Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
Published14 hours ago
Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.

item.title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
item.description:
Image source, Reuters / AFPImage caption,
Current polling suggests Gadi Eisenkot (left) is in a tight race with incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu (right) to become Israel's prime ministerPublished56 minutes ago
Israel's general election takes place on Tuesday 27 October.
It's the first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel and its subsequent conflicts in Gaza and with Iran, Hezbollah and the Houthis.
Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.
Who are the main contenders?
Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.
Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.
He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.
Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.
Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. item.title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick Jackson, Marco Silva and Thomas Copeland, BBC Verify Published21 October 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.
Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.
Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".
It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.
Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.
Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.
Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.
The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.
Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

item.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
item.description:
Image source, EPAImage caption,
Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this yearByKali HaysTechnology reporterPublished21 October 2026
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".
Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.
The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.
New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.
New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.
Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.
